#733. Michael Jackson’s ‘Thriller’ Scares Up Highest Rank on Billboard 200 Albums Chart in More Than 40 Years

The classic, which spent 37 weeks at No. 1 in 1983-84, surged sparked by Halloween.

Michael Jackson’s Thriller vaults 13-2 on the Billboard 200 (dated Nov. 14), scoring its highest rank on the list since the spring of 1984, when it logged its 37th and final week at No. 1 on the April 14-dated list. Thriller continues to hold the record for the most weeks atop the list for an album by a singular artist. (Only the film soundtrack to West Side Story spent more weeks at No. 1: 54, in 1962-63.)

The Billboard 200 chart ranks the most popular albums of the week in the U.S. based on multi-metric consumption as measured in equivalent album units, compiled by Luminate. Units comprise album sales, track equivalent albums (TEA) and streaming equivalent albums (SEA). Each unit equals one album sale, or 10 individual tracks sold from an album, or 2,500 ad-supported or 1,000 paid/subscription on-demand official audio and video streams generated by songs from an album. The new Nov. 14, 2026-dated chart will be posted in full on Billboard‘s website on Nov. 10. For all chart news, follow @billboard and @billboardcharts on both X and Instagram.

In the tracking week of Oct. 30 through Nov. 5 — thus, including Halloween — Thriller earned 55,000 equivalent album units (up 89%), boosted by seasonal spooky streams of the set’s title track, as well as new physical versions of the album that were released. Of that unit total, SEA units comprise 32,000 (up 37%, equaling 34.34 million on-demand official streams of the set’s songs; it moves 14-5 on Top Streaming Albums), album sales comprise 22,000 (up 335%; it rises 14-3 on Top Album Sales) and TEA units comprise 1,000 (up 30%).

On Oct. 30, Thriller was reissued across three new vinyl variants (two color editions and a liquid-filled version) and a cassette tape. The album’s 22,000 sales for the week mark its largest single-week sales sum in nearly four years, since it shifted 23,000 (Dec. 31, 2022-dated list).

Notably, of Thriller’s 22,000 sold in the latest tracking week, vinyl purchases account for 19,000 — the album’s largest sales week on vinyl since Luminate began electronically tracking sales in 1991.

With Thriller’s jump to No. 2, Jackson has his highest rank on the Billboard 200 in more than a decade, since the posthumous album Xscape debuted and peaked at No. 2 on the May 31, 2014-dated chart.

Notably, Thriller has appeared on the Billboard 200 each year since 2009, following Jackson’s death that June. It has resided in the top 20 each week since early May, with 15 consecutive weeks in the top 10 through August, spurred by the record-setting biopic Michael.

#732. Taylor Swift and Karlie Kloss Attend Travis Kelce’s Chiefs Game in Kansas City

The longtime friends reunited to watch the Chiefs take on the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium on Nov. 8.

Taylor Swift had some familiar company as she cheered on husband Travis Kelce and the Kansas City Chiefs on Sunday (Nov. 8).

The 36-year-old pop superstar watched the Chiefs take on the New York Jets at Arrowhead Stadium in Kansas City, joined by longtime friend Karlie Kloss. The supermodel, 34, was also among the guests at Swift and Kelce’s July 3 wedding at Madison Square Garden in New York City.

Swift and Kloss appeared in good spirits as they watched the Chiefs take the field for their ninth game of the season. The “Shake It Off” singer wore a red sweater as she cheered on Kelce alongside her parents, Andrea and Scott Swift. Sunday’s matchup also marked a career milestone for the tight end, who made his 200th NFL appearance.

Swift and Kloss first struck up a friendship in 2013, eventually becoming close enough to share the cover of Vogue in 2015. Their relationship later became the subject of speculation when they were seen together less frequently. In August 2023, Kloss attended Swift’s Eras Tour show in Los Angeles.

Sunday marked Swift’s fourth appearance at a Chiefs game this season. She previously attended the team’s Oct. 18 home game against the Los Angeles Chargers, watching from a suite alongside musician Este Haim and basketball star Caitlin Clark.

Earlier in the season, Swift attended the Chiefs’ Sept. 14 game against the Denver Broncos, where she was spotted with actor Tom Cruise. She returned to Arrowhead Stadium on Sept. 20 for the team’s matchup against the Indianapolis Colts.

Swift’s Oct. 18 appearance at Arrowhead Stadium came just one day after a surprise appearance at the 2026 Academy Museum Gala in Los Angeles, where she delivered the live debut of “The Fate of Ophelia” during a short set. The event honored filmmaker John Carpenter, Colman Domingo and Charlize Theron.

#731. What the rift within the Tsikhanouski family means for the Belarusian opposition in exile

Siarhei Tsikhanouski criticizes the work of his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, and her office. He also questions her legitimacy. What are the implications for Belarusian political forces in exile?

Blogger and dissident Siarhei Tsikhanouski , 48, was detained in Belarus in May 2020, after he had announced to challenge the country's ruler, Alexander Lukashenko, in the upcoming presidential elections. In December 2021, Tsikhanouski was convicted to 18 years in prison, in part for organizing "mass unrest."

After his arrest his wife, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya, took his place and challenged Lukashenko as presidential candidate. Despite allegations of large-scale vote-rigging, Lukashenko was declared the winner of the election in August 2020. This triggered unprecedented mass protests across the country. They were violently suppressed, and thousands of government critics were arrested or fled into exile. Tsikhanouskaya also fled her homeland and became the leading representative of the Belarusian democratic movement.

In June 2025, Siarhei Tsikhanouski was released after nearly five years in prison and was forcibly taken out of the country.

Some 14 months after his release, the blogger has re-activated his YouTube channel, where he not only denounces Alexander Lukashenko's regime, but also Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's office, Belarusian media in exile, political analysts and others. Thousands of people follow his streams.

In one of them, Tsikhanouski claims that while Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya obviously enjoyed "a certain legitimacy from the European Union," the people who were living "quietly and silently" in Belarus today had not granted her any. He said that many of those who had voted for her as joint candidate of Belarus' opposition were regretting this today.

Tsikhanouski has suggested that a supervisory board should be established under the label "United Office of Demoratic Forces." It would be made up of "former presidential candidates, protest leaders and iconic figures of the revolution," including himself and his wife. "There would not be a full legitimacy but one which was at least granted by Belarusians," Tsikhanouski said, adding that such a supervisory board could oversee the distribution of grant funds.

Speaking about his wife, he said: "Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya was a so-called technical candidate, who received the votes of all those who were against Lukashenko. The percentage of votes she received in the 2020 election was negligible because no one knew who she was. She was allowed to run because she did not pose a threat for the regime, and because she had neither supporters nor political experience."

Asked by DW what his goals were, Siarhei  Tsikhanouski refused to comment and referred to his livestreams instead. The former political prisoner is residing in the US and is, by his own account, currently unemployed. At the beginning of summer he said he was living in Los Angeles, learning English, preparing for university studies and writing a book. It is also known that his children — a teenage son and a younger daughter — temporarily stayed with him in the US. Today, however, they attend school in Poland, where Tsikhanouskaya resides.

Neither she nor her office have commented on the family situation or her husband's allegations. Even before the public dispute, the leader of the Belarusian democratic forces avoided commenting on her husband. Asked about his activities, she often suggested to approach him directly.

Speaking to DW in December 2025, Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya merely said: "What happens in the public sphere and what happens at home, are different things. I understand Siarhei's deep traumatization and also his very strong reactions to certain events. Siarhei was in prison for five years, and I look at it with great understanding. This is why I'm not going public or making any comments. We'll deal with it among ourselves."

During the 32-year-long rule of the Lukashenko regime, the Belarusian opposition has weathered many crises and conflicts. Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's leadership role has been called into question more than once. However, she and her team have always managed to work themselves out of difficult situations during the last couple of years. But will she still be able to do that now, with her own husband having turned into her critic?

Siarhei Tsikhanouski had gone back to his own self, said political scientist Yury Drakakhrust: "With all his idiosyncrasies, his style of debate, which is not exactly in line with common practice. This is likely to strike many as odd, including Sviatlana Tsikhanouskaya's international partners."

Tsikhanouski, Drakakhrust pointed out, insisted that he was the key figure of the 2020 events, which is why he was entitled to all the benefits, privileges, recognition and invitations. But there was no way back.

"Even if we assume that Tsikhanouski is right, that he was the central figure, what good would it do today?" he asked. "If, suddenly, hundreds of thousands of Belarusians watched his livestreams, collected funds, formed local groups or associations in Tsikhanouski's name, then perhaps it would be possible to turn back the wheel. But this will hardly be the case."

Drakakhrust described the current situation within the democratic forces as a "crisis." He doubted that Tsikhanouski would be able to reach an agreement with all the members of the supervisory board he has proposed. Furthermore, his wife, in particular, had since established certain assets, resources, and a status for herself through her office.

"Tsikhanouskaya is being received at high levels, if not as an elected president, then as a leader for Belarus and Belarusian democracy. She's not regarded as just one of several democratic leaders from Belarus," the political scientist said.

He pointed out that not only Tsikhanouskaya, but also other actors from the 2020 election campaign are in exile. They, however, had not achieved a similar level of representation or comparable access to resources. "She has surpassed them as a politician, and that's what counts."

Drakakhrust said that the Belarusian government views disputes among the opposition with a touch of irony, occasionally adding fuel to the fire: "Basically, they don't care who wins. The main thing is that there is conflict, bickering and mutual vilification."

#729. NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins is the 1st Black woman to command a space mission. Will we see more diversity in the future on the final frontier?

When Jessica Watkins became commander of her mission to the International Space Station, she didn't just fulfill her duty as an astronaut — she made history.

Watkins is commanding SpaceX's Crew-13 mission, which launched her and three other astronauts to the International Space Station on Oct. 1. As their Crew Dragon capsule lifted off atop a Falcon 9 rocket that day, Watkins became the first Black woman to command a crewed mission to space. Spaceflight and space science are historically white and male-dominated fields, so this milestone carries incredible significance.

"This is certainly an important milestone, I think both for our agency and for the country," Watkins said in a press briefing ahead of Crew-13's launch.

This is Watkins' second spaceflight. She previously flew on SpaceX's Crew-4 mission in 2022 and has spent more than 200 days in space to date, though that number will keep climbing for a while, as Crew-13 is set to be an approximately six-month mission. A geologist, astronaut, aquanaut and former professional rugby player, Watkins brings an incredible variety of skills to her new role as mission commander. And, in addition to what she's bringing to her colleagues on mission, she's also providing some serious inspiration for those back on Earth.

"Jessica is an inspirational symbol to a lot of people," commercial astronaut and fellow geologist Sian Proctor, who became the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft on SpaceX's private Inspiration4 mission to orbit in September 2021, told Space.com. Sian shared that the two even crossed paths years ago, when their astronaut training aligned.

"It just means so much to so many people when you see a diverse crew, and particularly women, and women of color, in leadership positions," Proctor said. "And it means something for America."

The visibility of Watkins' accomplishments and missions carries significant cultural weight. However, in addition to recognizing her many achievements, "you also should celebrate the fact that she's African American and a role model for her community," Proctor said.

Proctor, who similarly made spaceflight history with her mission, sees Watkins' role in Crew-13 as potentially more than just an exciting moment. Hopefully, she said, it will help lay the foundation for a more diverse future in human spaceflight.

"When they announced Jessica, I was super excited because it shows progress," Proctor said, sharing that she finds incredible importance in the "idea of looking at your crew and recognizing the fact that diversity makes the crew stronger."

While Watkins' historic milestone has been celebrated on social media and across the broader media landscape, NASA did not make a public statement commemorating the historic achievement. However, the agency confirmed its pioneering nature in an email to Space.com.

"NASA astronaut Jessica Watkins launched on her second spaceflight on Oct. 1, 2026, as commander of the agency's SpaceX Crew-13 mission to the International Space Station, becoming the first Black woman to command a crewed space mission," a NASA spokesperson wrote in the email.

"Watkins was selected as commander of Crew-13 based on her spaceflight experience, leadership, and ability to help the mission accomplish its objectives," the spokesperson added. "As a member of NASA's astronaut corps, she represents the best of America's talent, dedication, and spirit of exploration."

To date, the U.S. and the Soviet Union are the only nations to have launched Black astronauts into space. (The Soviets beat the U.S. to this milestone, launching Cuba's Arnaldo Tamayo Méndez in 1980. NASA's Guion Bluford became the first Black American in space three years later.) But, as Proctor shared, perhaps moments like this could serve to inspire other nations to follow suit.

"We can be a leader in saying, Look, if your country is diverse and has people from all different backgrounds, you should be encouraging them to apply and have a chance to be selected," Proctor said.

And, as a commercial astronaut herself, Proctor added that commercial space can continue to play a vital role in diversifying spaceflight.

"Jared did not even hesitate when he offered me the mission pilot seat for Inspiration4," Proctor said of her own selection as mission pilot by Jared Isaacman, the tech billionaire who funded and commanded the SpaceX mission. He now serves as NASA administrator.

"Commercial space has opened up so much opportunity and access. We are celebrating that because that's another way in which the space industry has diversified so much," Proctor added. "You can look at the history of space exploration and who's had access, and then you look at what commercial's done in the last five years, and it's incredible."

On the topic of the future of space exploration, Proctor expressed confidence that future crewed moon landings with NASA's Artemis program will be diverse.

"NASA is going to send diverse crews to the moon because they've done a good job of selecting diverse individuals with different heritages in their background," she said. NASA's current astronaut corps is roughly 45% women and 25% people of color. However, to-date only 6 Black women (including Watkins) have ever flown to space.

"Do I want to see more? Do I want women of color? Absolutely. They only have two Black women," Proctor said. But with the current diversity in NASA's astronaut corps as well as the continued development of commercial spaceflight, she is optimistic about a diverse future on the moon.

So far, NASA's Artemis program has been making some inroads when it comes to diversity. With Artemis II, we saw four people launch to the moon which included Victor Glover, the first person of color to ever travel beyond low-Earth orbit, and mission specialists Christina Koch and Jeremy Hansen who became the first woman and first non-American to make the same leap.

In reaching her own historic milestone as the first Black woman to pilot a spacecraft, Proctor understands that a historic moment like this carries not just incredible significance but a fair amount of personal pressure as well.

"If something goes wrong, because of who you are, maybe your gender or your ethnicity or race, you're looked at differently," she said. "When it goes right, you're not necessarily celebrated. But if it goes wrong, then that [adds to] that whole idea of 'not being qualified,'" that can come from prejudice.

"Because of who you are and the community you represent, you become the scapegoat," she added. "So, there's pressure to not have things go wrong and do everything you can to be better than the best."

But whether or not these pressures weigh on Watkins' mind, "we're all celebrating" back on Earth, Proctor said. "We're proud of her."

Chelsea Gohd served as a Senior Writer for Space.com from 2018 to 2022 before returning in 2026, covering everything from climate change to planetary science and human spaceflight in both articles and on-camera in videos. With a M.S. in Biology, Chelsea has written and worked for institutions including NASA JPL, the American Museum of Natural History, Scientific American, Discover Magazine Blog, Astronomy Magazine, and Live Science. When not writing, editing or filming something space-y, Gohd is writing music and performing as Foxanne, even launching a song to space in 2021 with Inspiration4. You can follow her online @chelsea.gohd and @foxanne.music

#728. Druski’s Best ‘SNL’ Sketches Had Him Singing Through a Proposal Gone Wrong & In a Hip-Hop Parody

The comedian hit the right beats while hosting 'SNL' for the first time Saturday night (Nov. 7).

Druski made his SNL hosting debut on an episode that had The Strokes as musical guest, but it was Druski crooning “she said yes” at the just the right comedic moment that was the real earworm of the show.

“Proposal” and “Golden Age of Hip-Hop,” two of the funniest sketches to make it to air Saturday night (Nov. 7), had the SNL host showing he’s got a knack for musical comedy — and some vocal talent.

In “Proposal,” SNL‘s Jeremy Culhane plays a man asking his girlfriend (Sarah Sherman) to marry him, and things don’t quite go as planned. But since he assumed she’d say yes and went all-out on making the proposal an unforgettable moment, the show goes on for his hired entertainment — Druski, expertly leading an awkward musical finale that was meant to celebrate the engagement.

“I don’t really know how to tell you this, but the next four minutes are about to be really tough,” Culhane says when Sherman turns him down.

And then all eyes (and ears) are on Druski and an ensemble that keeps growing around him as he belts with soul: “She said yes, oh, she said yes/ Can’t wait to see her wearing that dress/ Got down on one knee and she said yes.”

One of the other highlights of the episode was the final sketch, “Golden Age of Hip-Hop,” a TV documentary-style parody telling the story of a “socially conscious hip-hop” group called Lenny & The Street Smart Crew (Druski, James Austin Johnson, Ben Marshall, Kam Patterson and Tommy Brennan). The bit has the Druski-led crew performing songs like “Gangs Ain’t Good (Free Yo Mind)” and “You Can Be My Brother, Friend.”

When Druski was announced as a season 52 host for Saturday Night Live, he got plenty of support from his hip-hop friends. Among those sending him congratulatory comments were Drake, Travis Scott, Quavo and Wheezy.

#727. Morgan Wallen, Garth Brooks, Taylor Swift & More Artists With Most Weeks at No. 1 on Top Country Albums Chart: Full List

Male solo artists dominate, though three female solo artists and two groups have also achieved the feat.

Morgan Wallen’s I’m the Problem leads Billboard‘s Top Country Albums chart (dated Nov. 14) for the 52nd nonconsecutive week. This ups Wallen’s career tally of weeks at No. 1 to 238, allowing him to extend his lead as the artist with the most weeks at No. 1 in the chart’s 62-year history.

Wallen’s achievement is especially impressive because he has amassed this hefty total of weeks at No. 1 in such a short amount of time. He first topped the chart a little more than six years ago — on Aug. 15, 2020.

I’m the Problem is Wallen’s third album to log a full year at No. 1 on Top Country Albums. Dangerous: The Double Album clung to the top spot for 97 weeks from 2021-23. One Thing at a Time led for 87 weeks from 2023-25.

Top Country Albums originated as Hot Country Albums in the Jan. 11, 1964 issue of Billboard. Johnny Cash’s Ring of Fire (The Best of Johnny Cash) headed the inaugural chart. The compilation was well-timed: “Ring of Fire” had headed Hot Country Songs for seven weeks the previous summer and had crossed over to reach the top 20 on the Billboard Hot 100.

The chart was named Hot Country LP’s from 1968 to 1984, when vinyl LPs were king.

Twenty-one artists have logged 50 or more weeks at No. 1 on Top Country Albums. Male solo artists dominate, as you might expect, though three female solo artists have achieved the feat, as have two groups. (One of those groups is an all-female group.) Only one Black artist has amassed 50 or more weeks at No. 1, though that may change as country becomes more inclusive.

Here’s a look at all artists who have topped Top Country Albums for 50 or more weeks.

Longest-running No. 1: When the Sun Goes Down (14 weeks in 2004)

Notes: Chesney’s tally of No. 1 albums includes two live albums, LIVE: Live Those Songs Again (2006) and Live in No Shoes Nation (2017).

Longest-running No. 1: Blue (28 weeks in 1996-97)

Notes: Rimes’ total includes a 1997 compilation of early recordings, Unchained Melody: The Early Years. Rimes was just 14 in February 1997 when she won a Grammy for best new artist. She remains the youngest winner ever in that category.

Longest-running No. 1: My World (17 weeks in 1965-66)

Notes: My World was the first country album to receive a Grammy nod for album of the year. The album included the crossover hit “Make the World Go Away,” which all but defined the “countrypolitan” sound.

Longest-running No. 1: Wichita Lineman (20 weeks in 1968-69)

Notes: Wichita Lineman is tied with Johnny Cash at San Quentin for the longest run at No. 1 of any album in the 1960s. Campbell’s tally of No. 1 albums also includes Bobbie Gentry & Glen Campbell, a collab with the singer of “Ode to Billie Joe.” The 1968 album was the first collaborative album to reach No. 1 on the chart.

Longest-running No. 1: Pancho & Lefty (with Willie Nelson) (eight weeks in 1983)

Notes: Haggard’s tally of No. 1s includes eight albums on which his backing group, The Strangers, was also credited. Hag’s tally includes three live albums, Okie From Muskogee (1970), The Fightin’ Side of Me (1970)and I Love Dixie Blues … So I Recorded ‘Live’ in New Orleans (1973). It also includes two collabs with Willie Nelson, Pancho & Lefty and Django and Jimmie (2015).

Most recent week at No. 1: April 12, 2014

Longest-running No. 1: Johnny Cash at San Quentin (20 weeks in 1969)

Notes: Cash’s No. 1 albums spanned more than 50 years. Johnny Cash at San Quentin (which received a Grammy nod for album of the year) has had the longest run at No. 1 of any live album. It is also tied with Glen Campbell’s Wichita Lineman as the longest-running No. 1 album of the 1960s. Cash also reached No. 1 with two other live albums – Johnny Cash at Folsom Prison (1968) and The Johnny Cash Show (1970), which was recorded at the Grand Ole Opry. He also topped the chart with a 1985 collab LP with Willie Nelson, Waylon Jennings and Kris Kristofferson and with two posthumous albums – American V: A Hundred Highways (2006) and Out Among the Stars (2014).

Most recent week at No. 1: April 20, 1968

Longest-running No. 1: I’ve Got a Tiger by the Tail (15 weeks in 1965)

Notes: Owens’ first No. 1 album, Buck Owens Sings Tommy Collins (1964), was a tribute album to the singer/songwriter whose biggest hits included “You Better Not Do That” and “If You Can’t Bite, Don’t Growl.” Owens’ tally of No. 1 albums includes two live albums, Carnegie Hall Concert (1966) and Buck Owens and His Buckaroos in Japan! (1967).

Most recent week at No. 1: April 13, 2019

Longest-running No. 1s: Ocean Front Property (six weeks in 1987) and Carrying Your Love With Me (six weeks in 1997)

Notes: Strait made this list the hard way – without a single album that logged more than six weeks at No. 1. Strait’s tally of No. 1 albums includes the 1992 soundtrack to Pure Country, in which he starred.

Longest-running No. 1: Fly (36 weeks in 1999-2000)

Notes: The Chicks, formerly Dixie Chicks, are the second-highest ranking group on this list. Three of the group’s No. 1 albums – Fly, Home and Taking the Long Way – received Grammy nods for album of the year. The latter album won the award. The group’s most recent No. 1 album, Gaslighter, was bumped from the top spot by the debut album by a promising newcomer named Morgan Wallen.

Longest-running No. 1: Greatest Hits (16 weeks in 1979)

Notes: Jennings’ tally of No. 1 albums includes three collabs with Nelson – one just with Nelson; one that also included Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser; and one that included Johnny Cash and Kris Kristofferson as well. His tally also includes a 1976 live album, Waylon Live.

Longest-running No. 1: Not a Moment Too Soon (29 weeks in 1994)

Notes: McGraw’s tally includes a 2017 collab with his wife, Faith Hill, The Rest of Our Life. That title should probably be The Rest of Our Lives, but we’re not going to correct the grammar of someone who has logged 76 weeks at No. 1.

Longest-running No. 1: Always & Forever (43 weeks in 1987-88)

Notes: Always & Forever had the longest run at No. 1 of any album in the 1980s.

Longest-running No. 1s: Charley Pride Sings Heart Songs (16 weeks in 1972) and The Best of Charley Pride, Volume 2 (16 weeks in 1972).

Notes:  The albums referenced above were No. 1 back-to-back and spent a combined total of 32 consecutive weeks at No. 1. Now, that’s what you call dominating a chart. Both albums contained Pride’s signature song, “Kiss an Angel Good Mornin.’” Pride’s final No. 1 album, There’s a Little Bit of Hank in Me (1980), was a tribute to Hank Williams. Pride is the only Black artist on this list so far.

Longest-running No. 1: This One’s for You (50 weeks in 2017-18)

Notes: This One’s for You had the longest run at No. 1 of any album in the 2010s.

Longest-running No. 1: Come on Over (50 weeks in 1997-2000)

Notes: Twain is the second-highest ranking female solo artist on this list. Come on Over had the longest run at No. 1 of any album in the 1990s. The hit-studded blockbuster spent time at No. 1 in four consecutive years – 1997 through 2000. It received a Grammy nod for album of the year, and spawned two song of the year nominees, “You’re Still the One” and “You’ve Got a Way.”

Longest-running No. 1: Kenny (25 weeks in 1979-80)

Notes: Kenny, which housed the hit “You Decorated My Life,” had the longest run at No. 1 of any album in the 1970s. Rogers’ tally includes a 1978 collab with Dottie West, Every Time Two Fools Collide, and a 2018 compilation, The Best of Kenny Rogers: Through the Years, which hit No. 1 following his death in March 2020.

Most recent week at No. 1: July 29, 2023?

Longest-running No. 1: Fearless (35 weeks in 2008-09)

Notes:  Swift is the highest-charting female solo artist on this list, which is especially impressive given her mid-career pivot to pop. Her tally includes both the original and Taylor’s Version’s editions of Fearless, Speak Now and Red. With Fearless, Swift became the youngest Grammy winner for album of the year to that point, a title now held by Billie Eilish.

Longest-running No. 1: Always on My Mind (22 weeks in 1982)

Notes: Nelson’s tally includes a collab with Waylon Jennings, Jessi Colter and Tompall Glaser; another with Jennings, Johnny Cash and Kris Kristofferson; another with just Jennings, and two with Haggard. It also includes two live albums, Willie and Family Live (1979) and the Honeysuckle Rose soundtrack (1980).

Longest-running No. 1s: Feels So Right (28 weeks in 1981-82) and Mountain Music (28 weeks in 1982-83).

Notes: Alabama is the highest-ranking group on this list. Feels So Right (in May 1981) was the first No. 1 by a group that wasn’t named after its leader. (So, we’re discounting Merle Haggard and the Strangers, Sonny James and the Southern Gentlemen and The Charlie Daniels Band.) Alabama’s tally of No. 1 albums includes a 1988 live album, Alabama Live.

Longest-running No. 1: No Fences (41 weeks in 1990-91)

Notes: Brooks’ tally of No. 1 albums includes a double-disc live album, Double Live (1998); a pair of Christmas albums, Garth Brooks & the Magic of Christmas (1999) and Christmas Together (2016), the latter a collab with his wife, Trisha Yearwood; and a remarkable four box sets – The Limited Series (1998), Blame It All on My Roots: Five Decades of Influences (2013), The Ultimate Collection (2016) and The Anthology Part I: The First Five Years (2017).

Longest-running No. 1: Dangerous: The Double Album (97 weeks in 2021-23)

Notes: Dangerous: The Double Album had the longest run at No. 1 in the chart’s history. One Thing at a Time, which spent 87 weeks at No. 1, is in second place.

Spacewalks are hard work, so sometimes you need to take a break for a moment and snap a gorgeous selfie with your home planet in the background.

During a pre-Halloween spacewalk on Oct. 29, 2026, Canadian Space Agency astronaut Joshua Kutryk took a moment to pose for a photograph.

In this moment, the International Space Station to which he was tethered was orbiting 267 miles (430 kilometers) above the South Atlantic Ocean down below on Earth.

During this spacewalk — the first for a Canadian since 2019 — Kutryk and NASA astronaut Anil Menon worked together to install a new roll-out solar array on the station while also performing some "get ahead" tasks to prep for the next spacewalk, which is happening today (Nov. 5).

During today's excursion, the same two astronauts will venture out into space, tethered to the space station, to install the eighth and final roll-out solar array. These eight new arrays will boost the station's available power by a total of 30%, according to NASA officials.

When we think of astronauts working in space, we might think of the important science and research they're doing aboard the station. Astronauts work on everything from biomedical research to plant science and physics experiments. But the job also includes work on the space station itself.

Sometimes they have to venture out into the vacuum of space to fix urgent problems. These situations can be tense, and there's a lot of pressure to get things absolutely right.

But even spacewalks that do relatively mundane maintenance work, like the one on Oct. 29, come with pressure. Every minute that astronauts spend outside of the space station, there are countless risk factors floating around. Earth orbit is a very harsh environment, after all, even if it does allow for some pretty amazing selfies.

#725. Canadian PM Mark Carney discusses talks with the EU, overdependence on the US and how to deal with Donald Trump in a DW interview.

Prime Minister Mark Carney tells DW that Canada is seeking closer EU ties to "diversify and deepen" partnerships beyond the Americas. Despite German pushback, he said he favors the all-new term "associate membership."

Canadian Prime Minister Mark Carney spoke to DW on Friday after talks in Montreal with European Union leaders seeking to hammer out details of a new, closer partnership between Canada and the EU.

Amid difficult negotiations with US President Donald Trump, representing Canada's biggest trading partner, Carney said that he and his compatriots had come to realize the country was too dependent on the economic powerhouse to the south.

"The lesson we've taken, Canadians as a whole, is we're overdependent on the United States. Too closely connected to the United States. And we need to build our strength here at home and diversify and deepen our partnerships with like-minded countries internationally," Carney said.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

An EU delegation led by European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen and European Council President Antonio Costa held talks with Carney and other Canadian officials in Montreal on Friday.

They're discussing the plans floated by Commission President Ursula von der Leyen to forge what she called an "associate membership" — a status that does not yet exist for any other country — even as German Chancellor Friedrich Merz's government resists creating this label. Carney seemed to speak in its favor.

"Well, I think the advantage of what we're doing is that a few things are absolutely clear, irrespective of the exact terminology that's used. President von der Leyen uses associated membership. We use associated membership," he told DW's Katharina Kroll at Port of Montreal Tower.

"What does that mean? It means the closest possible partnership without being a full member of the European Union, because Canada is not in Europe geographically and therefore cannot have accession." Carney said.

Asked if he was looking to create a "new transatlantic bloc without the US," Carney said it was more about diversifying and deepening Canada's other partnerships than excluding by far its largest trading partner.

"We're both partners of the United States, obviously close partners, alliance partners in NATO. And there are many, many opportunities for cooperation with the United States," he said. "But in many cases, there'll be much deeper cooperation for Canada between Canada and Europe than Canada and the United States."

He mentioned both existing areas of cooperation like the Comprehensive Economic and Trade Agreement (CETA), calling it "one of the most successful free trade agreements in the world," and also pointed to research cooperation and programs like Horizon Europe and Erasmus+ enabling student exchanges.

But Carney also pointed to areas where the two sides could seek to expand cooperation, naming areas like space technologies, artificial intelligence and critical minerals.

Despite his well-documented difficulties with Donald Trump — perhaps most crudely exemplified by Trump's attempts to unilaterally rename Lake Ontario, or his posting AI videos imagining him as an ice hockey player beating Carney up in a fight — Carney said US-Canadian ties were too deep to be derailed by any governments or prime ministers or presidents.

"The bonds between Canadians and Americans are longstanding. They're very strong. And big elements of that will be maintained regardless of the government in Canada, the government in the United States, the combination of the two," he said.

Asked about the best way to deal with Trump, Carney said it was "to be direct, to be clear, to be absolutely clear about your bottom lines are." He said it was important to show respect but also to continue to bring "the negotiations back to the core issues."

But he said the tensions with Trump had demonstrated the need to diversify and to seek Canada's other most natural partners around the world.

He acknowledged that no matter the nature of the talks with the EU, "the scale of the relationship with the United States" would be "very hard to replace."

Asked if he was concerned that the talks could expose him to further tariffs or other punitive measures from the Trump administration, Carney said, "We've been living with this for some time."

"There have been many justifications for trade action against Canada that the United States has had," he said. "Our view is that all of them are unjustified under our trade agreement."

Carney said the crucial message, also for the Trump White House, was that the talks with Brussels concerned a "positive association" and partnership "to help solve global problems" and address global challenges.

"It's not against somebody. It's for. It's a positive act," he said.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this."

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Voyager, 1, humanity's most distant spacecraft, is back in contact after briefly losing touch with Earth last month.

The spacecraft stopped phoning home for about 48 hours between Oct. 18 and 20 due to a communications glitch that Voyager 1 resolved on its own, before engineers could send the long-running spacecraft a remote fix.

"This is the first time we've seen the spacecraft do something like this, but we are also at a point in the mission where we have to expect the unexpected," Kareem Badaruddin, Voyager mission manager at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL), said in an agency statement about the incident on Oct. 29.

Voyager 1 is almost one light-day from Earth, meaning that a command takes nearly a day to reach the spacecraft and a response takes another day to come back to our planet. The spacecraft will reach the light-day milestone on Nov. 18, at 16.09 billion miles (25.89 billion kilometers) from Earth.

NASA's Deep Space Network of three antennas does check-ins to make sure the spacecraft is doing well. On Oct. 18 and 19, Voyager 1 did not respond. Its signal fortunately reappeared on Oct. 20.

"Engineers still are investigating what caused the communication loss," JPL added in the statement, but said it appears Voyager 1 went into a sort of safe mode. "The team has so far determined that one group of thrusters went offline and their backups turned on. Such a swap is programmed to occur automatically if the spacecraft computers detect something amiss with the active thrusters."

Voyager 1 and its still-operational twin, Voyager 2, both launched in 1977 on an initial mission to explore planets in the solar system. The two spacecraft took advantage of a rare alignment that allowed them to swing from Jupiter to Saturn to Uranus and Neptune using a minimum of fuel, although funding to explore the more distant planets and moons was not guaranteed at launch.

The spacecraft duly swung by Jupiter's and Saturn's systems (some months apart from each other) to great acclaim before parting pathways. Voyager 1's close-up view of Saturn's rings as well as the moon Titan — which may have prebiotic or pre-life chemistry — altered the spacecraft's trajectory to put it high above the plane of the solar system. Meanwhile, Voyager 2 flew on to Uranus and Neptune in 1986 and 1989, respectively, providing the only up-close view of these planetary systems to date.

Running on nuclear power, and continuing to deliver valuable science from deep space, the Voyagers saw their missions extended repeatedly. Both crossed into interstellar space a few years ago, and are still operational.

But with age comes a cost: the plutonium power sources on both spacecraft are diminishing, requiring engineers to periodically shut off instruments or come up with other clever ways of saving power. Voyager 1 just underwent one of those power adjustments, nicknamed the "Big Bang" because it reconfigured a number of spacecraft instruments.

"In early September, engineers successfully turned off three devices on the Voyager 1 spacecraft and substituted them with three lower-power alternatives," JPL wrote of the effort, noting that Voyager 2 also had a "Big Bang" about six weeks previous to that.

JPL did not provide an estimate for how long the missions could keep running, but noted each spacecraft loses four watts of power a year — each launched with 470 watts — and that the spacecraft could continue operating science instruments "longer than previously anticipated" due to the Big Bang. On Voyager 1, for example, the falling power would have otherwise meant switching off another instrument possibly as soon as next summer.

In 2022, Suzanne Dodd, project manager for Voyager at JPL, stated the hope was the mission would continue to operate into the 2030s.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.

#722. Preprint platform offers to pay researchers to review papers, but questions remain

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Paying researchers to review papers is seen as a potential solution to clearing the peer-reviewing backlog.Credit: UpPiJ/iStock via Getty

A preprint platform is paying researchers for reviewing preprints uploaded by other scientists, reigniting debates about whether peer reviewers should be paid.

XSci, which launched in September, will reward a reviewer with US$200 if they send their feedback within five days of accepting the task and $100 if they do so between five and ten days. The fee is covered by other researchers, who pay XSci to have their preprints reviewed by scholars. The preprint website, which does not publish a journal, charges each author $399 for a round of review or $249 if they make their review report public.

The system enables authors to receive comments quickly while compensating reviewers for their time and effort, says Shumiao Ouyang, the founder of XSci, the start-up firm incorporated in Delaware that runs the platform. The company has received around $500,000 from private investors and is trying to raise more funds, Ouyang says.

A publishing platform that places code front and centre

A publishing platform that places code front and centre

“What authors get is an answer, usually within about five to ten days, to the question they care about most: does this paper have a real chance at the journals I am aiming at? Today, that answer can take months, and in some fields, years,” says Ouyang, who is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK. XSci also charges authors up to $19 to have their preprints reviewed by a range of artificial-intelligence programs, although access to some AI tools is free.

Several researchers interviewed by Nature say that XSci’s business model is interesting, but that its future will depend mostly on whether it can attract authors to use its human-reviewing service.

“Will authors be willing to pay such a fee? Where does the money come from?” asks developmental biologist and toxicologist Daniel Gorelick at Baylor College of Medicine in Houston, Texas, who has served as editor-in-chief of Biology Open since July 2023.

But Gorelick also says that cash payments are “a powerful incentive”. Biology Open, an open-access journal published by The Company of Biologists, has been paying reviewers £220 (or $280) per manuscript since 2024 through a programme called Fast and Fair. The payment is issued to the reviewer if they send in their work on time and if its quality meets the editors’ expectations.

Ouyang expects XSci’s core authors to be doctoral and postdoctoral students, as well as early-career researchers “who often cannot wait for a year or more for a journal’s decision”.

Peer reviewers are conventionally expected to review manuscripts as a service to the scientific community, rather than for a fee. By paying them at the preprint stage, Ouyang says, XSci intends to tackle challenges that dog the academic publishing industry today: how to convince scholars to review the work of others and to do it quickly.

Several studies1–3 have shown that journal editors are finding it increasingly difficult to source reviewers for various reasons, including a rising number of submissions and academics’ growing workloads. These and other issues often lead to a long review time, which can range from a few weeks to several months.

XSci states on its website that academics can register their interest to be paid reviewers. But in reality, says Ouyang, a scholar must be invited by the website to review a manuscript. The website nevertheless has a ‘register interest’ field for practical reasons because, he explains, “it tells us how many willing researchers there are in each field.”

Shumiao Ouyang is an economist at the University of Oxford, UK, and founder of XSci.Credit: Yizhen Zhang

Ouyang says that XSci has developed an AI program to help find suitable reviewers quickly. Once an author uploads their manuscript to XSci and chooses the human-reviewing option, the AI tool will compile a ranking of potential reviewers by screening candidates from three sources: the scientists who wrote the papers that the manuscript cites, those scholars’ regular collaborators and researchers who have published papers on similar topics in the author’s target journals. The AI program will rank, then e-mail, potential reviewers one by one. Each potential reviewer has 12 hours to accept the job, says Ouyang.

If the reviewer thinks that the manuscript could be published in the author’s target journals after reasonable changes, the preprint will be given a badge on the website, demonstrating that it has been reviewed and is endorsed by the reviewer.

In time, XSci hopes to form partnerships with journal publishers that would allow the journals’ editors to use XSci’s review reports as part of their assessments. This would happen only if the authors and reviewers both agree to the reports being shared, Ouyang says. The idea is that editors can decide what to do with XSci’s reviews: whether to use them to replace one round of their own reviews or as external references, he adds. In follow-up questions from Nature, however, Ouyang stressed that the badge would merely “become useful information for an editor”.

“Whether a journal gives them any weight is the entirely the journal’s decision,” he added.

In 2025, Fast and Fair helped to slash the time that Biology Open editors spent making the first decision about a manuscript from an average of 37.7 working days under the free-reviewing route to an average of 5.5 working days, according to a preprint co-authored by Gorelick4. The programme also led to review invitations having a higher acceptance rate and a higher completion rate of accepted tasks, the study found.

But a separate study found that paying reviewers did not achieve substantial improvements. Editors at Critical Care Medicine, a journal published by Lippincott Williams & Wilkins, carried out a six-month experiment in which they sent reviewers invitations with or without monetary incentives in alternating two-week blocks5. They found that 50% of review invitations with a $250 cash reward resulted in a peer-review report in 14 days, compared with 42% of invitations without the fee. Paid reviewers also delivered their work just one day quicker on average than did non-paid reviewers.

“It didn’t move the needle too much,” says David Maslove, one of the editors who co-authored in the study and a clinician-scientist at Queen’s University in Kingston, Canada.

‘Getting paid to review is justice’: journal pays peer reviewers in cryptocurrency

‘Getting paid to review is justice’: journal pays peer reviewers in cryptocurrency

A paying system comes with challenges, researchers warn. There need to be stringent quality controls, as well as policies in place to ensure that reviewers don’t game the system and publishers don’t take advantage of reviewers, Gorelick says. “You can’t just pay reviewers and walk away,” he notes.

“XSci currently does not check the quality of the reviews done by the reviewers before they are released to the authors,” says Jeffery Poon, publishing and editorial lead of XSci. If the authors are not satisfied with what they receive, they can initiate an appeal through XSci, Poon notes. XSci plans to provide tools to reviewers to help them check their own work, but the team is still working out how that could be implemented in reality, he adds.

#721. Scientists smash oxygen nuclei to recreate matter from the Big Bang

New findings from the STAR experiment at the Relativistic Heavy Ion Collider (RHIC) suggest that scientists can recreate an extraordinary form of matter from the earliest moments of the universe using surprisingly small atomic collisions. By smashing oxygen nuclei together at nearly the speed of light, researchers have uncovered strong evidence of quark-gluon plasma (QGP), an extremely hot and dense state of matter that existed shortly after the Big Bang.

The findings, published in Physical Review Letters, reveal that high-energy streams of particles lose energy as they travel through the material created by these collisions. This effect, called jet quenching, provides an important clue that quark-gluon plasma has formed.

Scientists have previously observed jet quenching in collisions involving much larger atomic nuclei at RHIC, a U.S. Department of Energy (DOE) Office of Science User Facility that operated at Brookhaven National Laboratory from 2000 until 2026. The same effect has also been detected in oxygen collisions at CERN's Large Hadron Collider (LHC), the European Particle Physics Laboratory.

What makes the new RHIC findings especially significant is that the oxygen collisions occurred at substantially lower energies. The results establish a new lower boundary for the conditions known to produce quark-gluon plasma in this small collision system, helping scientists narrow down what it takes to create matter resembling that of the infant universe.

"The QGP is believed to be the form of matter that filled the early universe -- before the protons and neutrons that make up today's atoms formed. Understanding its properties is essential for uncovering how the early universe evolved in its first microseconds," said Li Yi, a professor of physics at Shandong University who oversaw the STAR analysis.

"One of the most powerful ways scientists study the QGP is by identifying where its signatures appear -- and just as importantly, where these signatures turn off," she said.

Rongrong Ma, a STAR physicist at Brookhaven Lab, explained why investigating smaller collisions is so valuable.

"This analysis is pushing the boundaries to an extreme case to help us learn something about this jet quenching phenomenon and the conditions needed to generate a QGP."

How Scientists Recreate Matter From the Early Universe

RHIC was designed specifically to produce and investigate quark-gluon plasma. Traditionally, researchers have accomplished this by accelerating gold nuclei to enormous speeds and crashing them into one another.

Each gold nucleus contains 79 protons and 118 neutrons. When two such nuclei collide with sufficient energy, the boundaries of their protons and neutrons effectively break down, releasing the quarks and gluons inside them. The tremendous energy of the impact also generates thousands of additional quarks and gluons through the conversion of energy into matter, as described by Einstein's famous equation, E=mc2.

The result is a fleeting droplet of primordial matter. It is smaller than an atomic nucleus and survives for less than a billionth of a billionth of a second. Almost immediately, the quarks and gluons recombine into more familiar particles.

Because this exotic substance disappears so quickly, scientists cannot examine it directly. Instead, they use enormous instruments such as the STAR detector to analyze the particles that emerge from the collision.

One particularly revealing clue comes from particles that escape with less energy than expected. Their reduced energy suggests they interacted with the dense mixture of quarks and gluons before escaping.

Researchers pay special attention to jets, which are narrow sprays of extremely energetic particles. These often originate when a quark or gluon from one nucleus strikes a quark or gluon from another, sending two particle jets traveling in opposite directions.

If these paired jets, known as "di-jets," form near the edge of the collision region, one may have to travel farther through the plasma than the other. Comparing their behavior allows scientists to investigate how the surrounding material drains energy from particles passing through it.

Yi offered a familiar comparison to explain the process.

"You can think of it like shooting a bullet through, say, water," Yi said. "Because of the resistance, the bullet will slow down. It's the same thing with these high-energy particles. When they go through the QGP, they will lose energy."

For decades, RHIC experiments have provided clear evidence of jet quenching in collisions between gold nuclei. The effect is especially noticeable in jets that travel longer distances through the newly created matter.

Scientists believe these particles lose more energy because they encounter more quarks and gluons before escaping. Jets originating closer to the outer boundary generally pass through less material and experience fewer interactions.

These measurements helped establish that RHIC was successfully producing quark-gluon plasma. Additional evidence came from several other experiments, including an unexpected discovery about how the resulting matter behaves.

Scientists observed that relatively low-energy particles emerging from gold collisions moved collectively, following coordinated patterns. This behavior indicated that the plasma flowed almost like a perfect liquid, with extraordinarily little viscosity or internal resistance.

The discovery was a major surprise when researchers first identified it. Collective flow has since become another important "smoking gun" signature of quark-gluon plasma.

Can Tiny Atomic Collisions Create Primordial Matter?

After establishing these signatures in collisions involving large nuclei, physicists began finding similar collective motion in much smaller systems.

Experiments at the LHC, followed by studies at RHIC, detected collective flow when tiny projectiles such as protons, deuterons, and helium-3 nuclei struck much larger gold or lead nuclei. Researchers at the LHC even observed comparable flow patterns in collisions between individual protons.

These results raised a major question. Did the coordinated particle motion mean that these much smaller collisions were also producing quark-gluon plasma, or could another mechanism explain the observations?

Scientists needed a more definitive sign.

"The next natural question is: Can you see jet quenching, the other key signature that QGP is formed, in these very small collision systems?" asked Brookhaven's Ma. "We haven't seen any unambiguous signal, so it's still kind of under debate in these small systems. We want to search for the smallest system where we can still see an unambiguous jet-quenching signal," he said.

To investigate, researchers turned to collisions between oxygen nuclei.

An oxygen nucleus contains just eight protons and eight neutrons, making it far smaller than the gold nuclei typically used in RHIC experiments. Oxygen nuclei also have a relatively symmetrical, spherical shape, which makes the geometry of their collisions easier to analyze.

"That means we can more easily look for signs of asymmetric quenching of di-jets produced close to the edge of the circular interaction region in head-on collisions," said Maowu Nie, an associate professor at Shandong University who contributed to the research.

The scientists could also examine how the outcome changed depending on whether the oxygen nuclei collided directly or merely grazed one another.

"We can also compare how jets behave in head-on central collisions -- those that produce the most particles and therefore have the highest likelihood of making a QGP -- with collisions where the two oxygen nuclei barely strike each other, which aren't expected to generate a QGP."

Nie explained that these grazing collisions are recognizable because they generate far fewer particles than direct impacts.

Oxygen Collisions Reveal a 20% Suppression

To search for jet quenching, the researchers developed an analysis that identifies concentrated streams of high-energy particles and measures how many emerge above a selected energy threshold.

"Our measurements are essentially counting experiments," said Sijie Zhang, who conducted the research for her master's thesis under Yi and Nie at Shandong University and is now pursuing a Ph.D. at Yale University.

"We have an algorithm that finds the collimated groups of high-energy particles, the jets, and we count how many of these particles above a certain energy threshold come out."

Yang He, a former Ph.D. student at Shandong University who developed the analysis framework and now studies oxygen collisions at the LHC, described how the team used different collision types to identify energy loss.

"We compare what we see in back-to-back jets produced near the edge of the system, and we compare what we see in head-on collisions with the counts in non-central collisions where we don't expect to see quenching."

The team analyzed STAR measurements from oxygen collisions conducted at RHIC in 2021, at a collision energy of 200 billion electron volts (GeV).

The results revealed a 20% suppression of high-energy particles associated with jet quenching.

Although this suppression was smaller than what physicists typically measure in gold collisions, that difference was expected because oxygen collisions generate much smaller systems.

Crucially, the observed effect was still strong enough to provide clear evidence that quark-gluon plasma had formed.

Comparing Big Bang Matter at Different Energies

Oxygen offers scientists another important advantage. Apart from proton-proton collisions, it is the only nuclear species that has been investigated in collisions at both RHIC and the LHC.

That gives researchers an unusual opportunity to make an "apples-to-apples" comparison between two facilities operating at very different collision energies.

The LHC carried out its first oxygen collisions in 2025. According to results reported by CERN, those experiments revealed both collective flow and jet quenching, providing additional indications that quark-gluon plasma can form in relatively small nuclear collisions.

However, the LHC operated at collision energies exceeding 5,000 GeV, far above the 200 GeV used in the RHIC measurements.

"With a higher energy collision, it's more likely to create more and more quarks and gluons and a hotter, denser QGP system," Yi said. "That means the jet quenching signal, if it's there, should be bigger at LHC compared to RHIC."

While higher energies make it easier to create the hot, dense conditions needed for quark-gluon plasma, lower-energy experiments may be more useful for determining precisely when those conditions are no longer sufficient.

By reducing the collision energy and using smaller nuclei, physicists can approach the threshold at which the distinctive signatures of primordial matter disappear.

"We are pushing the boundaries in two ways to explore the minimal conditions for creating a QGP, both in terms of the nucleus size by looking at these small oxygen-oxygen collisions, but also by looking at data from lower collision energies -- and we still see this crucial QGP signature. That's a unique feature of our measurement," Ma said.

New Experiments Could Reveal the Limits of Primordial Matter

Although RHIC has now completed its operations, scientists still have additional oxygen collision data to investigate.

During the collider's final experimental run, researchers collected measurements using both STAR and sPHENIX, RHIC's newest detector. The facility concluded its operations with oxygen collisions recorded by both instruments on February 6, 2026.

These remaining datasets could provide further insights into how small a collision system can become, and how low its energy can fall, before quark-gluon plasma can no longer form.

Understanding those limits may help physicists piece together the behavior of matter during the first microseconds of the universe, when quarks and gluons had not yet combined into the protons and neutrons that make up ordinary atoms today.

The research received financial support from the DOE Office of Science, the U.S. National Science Foundation (NSF), and additional international agencies and organizations identified in the scientific publication.

The researchers also used the Open Science Grid, which receives direct support from NSF, along with computing resources at Brookhaven Lab's Scientific Data and Computing Facilities and the National Energy Research Scientific Computing Center (NERSC), a DOE Office of Science User Facility located at DOE's Lawrence Berkeley National Laboratory.

After a record-breaking journey around the moon, Artemis 2 astronaut Victor Glover explains why you don't need to travel into space to see Earth differently.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

TENERIFE, Canary Islands — Imagine traveling over 250 million miles from home, watching Earth disappear behind the moon and losing contact with the billions of people who call it home. What would you miss most? For Artemis II astronaut Victor Glover, the answer wasn't a particular place, a familiar view or even the comforts of home. It was something much more fundamental: human connection.

Speaking during a discussion with former astronaut Chris Hadfield at the Starmus VIII festival on Oct. 18 in Tenerife, Canary Islands, Glover reflected on the extraordinary experience of traveling around the moon and how being so far from Earth had given him a renewed appreciation for the people living on it.

"The greatest reason to go to space, it isn't to be a swashbuckler hero," Glover said. "It's to do something that only 651 people have been able to do: miss Earth and miss other Earthlings."

Glover was one of the four astronauts aboard NASA's Artemis II mission, which launched on April 1, 2026, marking humanity's first crewed journey to the moon since Apollo 17 in 1972. Alongside NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman and Christina Koch and Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the crew traveled farther from Earth than any humans before them.

As the Orion spacecraft traversed the far side of the moon, the Artemis II crew watched Earth disappear below the lunar horizon before losing radio contact with our planet. Around 40 minutes later, Earth came back into view as the spacecraft emerged from behind the moon.

For Glover, however, the experience was about much more than the view. He believes that if everyone on Earth had the opportunity to make the same journey, they would come away with a similar appreciation for what they'd left behind.

"I think all of us would say something in our native language, in the most basic way we can communicate about love, joy, hope and inspiration," Glover said.

Although Glover shared the extraordinary journey with three fellow astronauts, the four of them were separated from the rest of humanity by hundreds of thousands of miles.

And for Glover, that distance brought with it a strange contradiction: the farther he traveled from humanity, the more he longed to connect with it."At the point of ultimate disconnection, [there is] this longing for connection," Glover said.

The experience gave him a perspective that he carried back into everyday life.

"There are moments where I am rushing through traffic and want to get where I'm going because I'm being selfish," Glover admitted. "But I don't have to stay there."

Instead, he remembers what it felt like to look back at a planet so distant that everyone who has ever lived could be covered by his hand.

"I wish you could all feel what it's like to come back home after that disconnection," he said.

Astronauts often describe experiencing the "overview effect", a profound shift in perspective that can come from seeing Earth from space. But Glover believes that there's something equally powerful waiting to be discovered much closer to home.

When asked by a Starmus VIII attendee whether people needed to undergo something extraordinary to develop a greater sense of kindness toward others, his answer was no.

Glover encouraged people to look more closely at the natural world around them, whether that meant walking along the beach, watching the ocean or simply examining a leaf held up to sunlight. Even something as ordinary as a leaf, he explained, is capable of turning sunlight into food through photosynthesis. And although science can explain how that happens, understanding the process doesn't make it any less remarkable.

"We have to choose to be moved by these things," Glover said.

He worries that modern life, with its endless technological distractions, has made it all too easy to overlook the extraordinary things happening around us.

"Familiarity breeds contempt. Have you heard this? I think it's worse than that. Familiarity breeds indifference," he said.

Glover has a name for this perspective he hopes people can rediscover without traveling into space: The sea level effect.

It's about finding the same sense of wonder and connection that astronauts experience in orbit, but right here on Earth, where most of us spend our lives. And ultimately, Glover believes the greatest wonder isn't the moon, the stars, or even the incredible complexity of nature. It's the people we share our planet with.

"I think the hardest place to see this miracle is in the actual greatest miracle in the universe: other humans," he said.

"We all feel it with babies, but when we get old enough to have opinions, we start to want to argue with each other."

Glover hopes that by taking the time to appreciate the natural world, people might become a little more willing to appreciate one another too.

"That's the mission that I want to be part of for the rest of my life," Glover said.

Daisy Dobrijevic joined Space.com in February 2022, having previously worked as a staff writer for All About Space magazine. She completed an editorial internship with BBC Sky at Night Magazine and worked at the National Space Centre, communicating space science to the public.

Daisy holds a PhD in plant physiology and a Master's in Environmental Science. Based in Nottingham, U.K., she covers all things space, with a special focus on solar activity and space weather. She also has a keen interest in astrotourism and is always on the lookout for the next northern lights adventure.

She will join Hurtigruten as an onboard astronomer for a northern lights sailing in January 2027.

#719. Embarrassing name? How we live with names we don't like

What happens when your name evokes laughter or ridicule? Research points to negative life outcomes, but some people learn to embrace unfortunate names.

As a child growing up in Australia, Louise Pain hated her surname.

"People used to tease me; I was called things like 'Pain in the a*s,'" she told DW. "I remember actively hating my surname when I was a child and wanting to change it."

The jokes have followed her throughout her life, even after she moved to Germany. But one thing did eventually change: Pain's feelings about her own name.

Names are not only a fundamental part of how we identify ourselves — they can, beyond teasing, also influence how other people treat us. So, what happens if we dislike our own name, or if it is perceived negatively by those around us?

"A person's name is vital to their sense of identity," psychoanalyst Mikita Brottman told DW. "When someone has an embarrassing name, that embarrassment can be incorporated into their identity."

Research on name bias has linked negatively perceived names with romantic rejection,as well as lower educational outcomes, lower self-esteem and more frequent smoking.

This suggests that names could influence our life trajectory, namely through self-esteem and opportunity.

But a person's relationship with their name is not necessarily fixed. Pain's lived experience, and that of another woman with the first name Tiny, shows how people can find ways to reclaim, and even come to value, names that once triggered ridicule and rejection.

Names can act as "signals" when you first meet someone, personality psychologist Jochen Gebauer told DW. Those signals may lose importance as people get to know each other, but Gebauer said their effects could also accumulate over a lifetime, potentially contributing to "real measurable advantages and disadvantages."

Research led by sociologist Anthony Lee found that a name can evoke inaccurate assumptions about intelligence, competence, trustworthiness, sociability and attractiveness. For Pain, other people's reactions have extended beyond jokes. In high school, a teacher refused to believe that 'Pain' was her real surname and reprimanded her in front of the class.

"Your name couldn't possibly be Pain. Write your real name!" she recalled the teacher saying.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

In Lee's UK-based research, less familiar names tended to fall along a dimension partly characterized as "weirdness," which may help explain why difficult-to-pronounce or culturally unfamiliar names receive more negative evaluations.

Tiny, now 54, encountered the same questions about her unfamiliar name growing up in Greece.

Her parents had adapted "Tiny" to "Tinie" to make it sound more Greek, but people would repeatedly ask what her real or baptismal name was.

Even relatives have refused to accept it. Recently, two elderly aunts introduced her to someone as "Haritini," a conventional Greek name.

"I didn't even bother correcting them at this point," Tiny told DW.

Tiny's relationship with her name has also evolved.

"The jokes [from others] got repetitive and boring pretty fast, so at least I was left with the sense that I have something unique with my name going on."

Pain, now 40, discovered how much cultural context could change the reaction to her surname when she began learning her father's native French as a teenager. In French, 'pain' means bread.

"People started calling me 'Bread! Louise Bread.'"

Later, after moving to Germany, the jokes became mostly bread-related rather than the more scathing ones she had experienced in Australia. "That helped me to feel better about my name," she said.

As they got older, both Pain and Tiny developed coping strategies to pre-empt people's reactions to their names.

Tiny sometimes introduces herself with: "Hi, I'm Tiny. It's my name and not a statement," or, "I'm Tiny. Not a difficult name to live up to."

"This usually stops people from asking awkward questions."

Pain also began to embrace the humor surrounding her name.

"I was convinced that I should become either a doctor or a dominatrix, or perhaps both, to become either 'Doctor Pain,' or 'Mistress Pain.'"

"Names can conjure that whole spectrum of shame and pride," psychoanalyst Melissa Daum told DW.

Pain now finds that people tend to see her surname as "funny and endearing… it's become something that is more of a funny talking point."

But the childhood discomfort has not entirely disappeared. When Pain thinks about having children, her feelings about the name become more complicated.

"I don't really want to pass on my surname ... so there is a deeper wound there."

But Pain also believes her father would be deeply hurt if future children had a different name. The surname she once hated connects her to him and to her French heritage.

"Something that once feels like an inconvenience or a source of self-consciousness can become a marker of distinctiveness, history, or belonging," Daum said.

"My parents seemingly made an unfortunate choice, but by now I have embraced both the name and the sense of uniqueness that comes with it."

That does not mean she uses Tiny everywhere. She avoids it on dating apps because "Tiny might give off the wrong message," and does not use it in her email address when she wants to appear professional.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Pain, meanwhile, uses a Germanized version of the French word for bread as her social media surname.

Online, people have more control over what name they present to others. As Daum put it: "Choosing one's own name can feel like an act of mastery, even a refusal of that original passivity: I will decide what I am called and how I am encountered."

But accepting a name does not necessarily mean embracing it in every situation.

Pain once wanted to change her surname. Tiny considered using her middle name in her thirties. Neither ultimately abandoned the names that had caused them difficulties.

For Tiny, at least, a name that once made her feel awkward has become something she can imagine carrying for the rest of her life.

"It might be cute to eventually be a granny called Tiny."
